lessons.title: Organize project photography around the change
lessons.principle: When real project photos exist, sequence them as a transformation the visitor can verify.
lessons.explanation: A trade or studio with several inspected job photos can lead with the outcome, then the work that produced it. The photo is evidence, not decoration.
useWhen: Two or more usable project photographs
The visitor needs to judge craft before contacting
avoidWhen: The only images are logos, icons, or uninspected downloads
requiredAssets: Inspected project photos with honest captions
contraindications: Fewer than two usable project images
lessons.visitorGoal: See whether this business has done the kind of work they need.
lessons.composition: One dominant before/after or finished-job plate, then a quieter supporting sequence.
lessons.typography: Short captions that name the job, not a slogan over the photograph.
lessons.media: Crop to the work. Do not cover the subject with a full-bleed headline.
lessons.mobile: Stack the outcome photo, then the caption, then the action. Do not crop the subject out of the frame.
lessons.adaptation: Pick the strongest inspected job for the first screen. Move the rest to a project index with the same caption system.
lessons.counterexample: A row of equal cards, each a different photo with the same 'View project' button.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: Equal cards hide which job is the proof the visitor came to judge.

references.note: Synthetic teaching pair, not a customer site.

lessons.title: Explain the process when images are scarce
lessons.principle: A specialist with little usable imagery should show the diagnostic or working sequence in type and structure.
lessons.explanation: Inventing stock photography makes the business look like every other template. A clear process is more specific than a fake hero photo.
useWhen: The offer is expertise, diagnosis, or a method
avoidWhen: A large inspected project library is the actual proof
requiredAssets: A real sequence of steps from the business evidence
contraindications: Requires a gallery of project photos
lessons.visitorGoal: Understand how the engagement works before asking for it.
lessons.composition: A numbered diagnostic column with one action, not a photo placeholder.
lessons.typography: The step names carry the hierarchy. Keep the display size for the offer, not for a missing image.
lessons.media: Use a diagram or a single inspected artifact only when it exists. Leave the space empty rather than fake.
lessons.mobile: Keep the step order identical to desktop. The action stays after the step that justifies it.
lessons.adaptation: Write the steps from harvested process facts. If a step is uncertain, omit it.
lessons.counterexample: A gray box labeled 'Your image here' beside three generic benefit cards.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The placeholder asks the visitor to imagine proof the business did not supply.

lessons.title: Put people next to the claim they substantiate
lessons.principle: A portrait or team fact belongs beside the responsibility it proves, not in a detached avatar row.
lessons.explanation: Inspected people photos and named roles help when the visitor is hiring a person. Unrelated headshots do not.
useWhen: Inspected portraits or named practitioners exist
The visitor is choosing a person or a small team
avoidWhen: No staff facts or portraits were harvested
requiredAssets: Named people with roles, or inspected portraits
lessons.visitorGoal: Know who will actually do the work.
lessons.composition: One practitioner with role, scope, and the work they are tied to.
lessons.typography: The person's name is secondary to what they do for this visitor.
lessons.media: Use only inspected portraits. Do not import faces from reference sites.
lessons.mobile: Name and role stay with the portrait. Do not dump every person into equal circles.
lessons.adaptation: If only one person is evidenced, design for one person. Do not invent colleagues.
lessons.counterexample: Six identical circular crops with first names and no responsibilities.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: Equal avatars imply a team the evidence does not describe.

references.note: Inspected first view: a portrait sits beside a large promise and three proof lines. The marketplace banner is capture chrome. The person and legal claims are not client facts.

lessons.title: Give unequal services unequal emphasis
lessons.principle: When one offer matters more to the visitor, the page should show that difference in scale and position.
lessons.explanation: A business with a primary service and several add-ons should not present them as the same card three times.
useWhen: Three or more services with different visitor importance
avoidWhen: The services are genuinely peers, such as equal menu categories
requiredAssets: A ranked or evidenced list of services
lessons.visitorGoal: Find the service that matches their job without reading every sibling.
lessons.composition: Primary offer in a large band. Secondary offers in a quieter index.
lessons.typography: One display headline for the primary offer. Secondary offers use the body scale.
lessons.media: Spend the strongest image on the primary offer only if that image exists.
lessons.mobile: The primary offer remains first. Secondary offers can become a short list.
lessons.adaptation: Rank from the narrative's visitor questions, not from an alphabetical menu.
lessons.counterexample: Three identical cards with the same button weight for a flagship service and two minor add-ons.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: Equal cards tell the visitor the business has no priority.

lessons.title: Make dense facts scannable
lessons.principle: Hours, specs, coverage, and requirements should be a structured reference, not a paragraph of adjectives.
lessons.explanation: Visitors with a practical question leave if the fact is buried in a hero slogan.
useWhen: The visitor job is to check a fact before acting
avoidWhen: The page is a single emotional introduction with no operational facts
requiredAssets: Harvested facts that are safe to publish
contraindications: Publishing an unverified price or hour
lessons.visitorGoal: Confirm the practical constraint that decides the visit or the call.
lessons.composition: A definition list or table with a stable label column.
lessons.typography: Labels and values in one size system. Do not set specifications in display type.
lessons.media: Optional. A diagram helps only when it is clearer than the list.
lessons.mobile: Keep each fact as label plus value. Do not turn the list into equal marketing cards.
lessons.adaptation: Publish only facts with evidence. Mark conflicts instead of averaging them.
lessons.counterexample: A hero headline that paraphrases the hours and hides the actual schedule.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The visitor cannot extract the fact without rereading marketing copy.

references.note: Synthetic teaching pair. Apex's inspected first view also puts a practical estimate panel on a work photo; that panel is a reference, not a template.

lessons.title: Show the material at a readable scale
lessons.principle: Products and materials need to be identifiable. A tiny swatch or a text-covered photo fails that job.
lessons.explanation: If the business sells a physical thing, the visitor is judging texture, portion, or finish.
useWhen: Inspected product or material images exist
avoidWhen: The business has no product photography and the offer is a service process
requiredAssets: Inspected images where the material is legible
contraindications: Images are low-resolution or covered in baked-in text
lessons.visitorGoal: Recognize the product or material before ordering or visiting.
lessons.composition: A large plate of the object with a short identifying caption.
lessons.typography: Keep type off the important part of the object.
lessons.media: Do not upscale a tiny asset to fill the viewport.
lessons.mobile: The object remains large enough to identify after stacking.
lessons.adaptation: If the asset is weak, say so in the storyboard and use type instead of enlarging it.
lessons.counterexample: A full-bleed photo with a centered headline covering the product.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The visitor cannot see the thing they would buy.

references.note: Inspected 375px first view: the words 'smash burgers' sit above a large food photograph, with a Menu control. Capture includes a theme-marketplace banner that is not the restaurant.

lessons.title: Answer the visit before the atmosphere
lessons.principle: A place people must travel to should expose hours, address, and access as early as the mood.
lessons.explanation: Atmosphere can support the visit. It cannot replace the facts that decide whether the visit is possible.
useWhen: The business has a location, hours, menu, or access instructions
avoidWhen: The business does not serve visitors at a place
requiredAssets: Harvested address, hours, or access facts
contraindications: Requires a full menu the source does not contain
lessons.visitorGoal: Decide if they can get there, and when.
lessons.composition: Practical facts in a stable block. Photography supports, it does not replace the facts.
lessons.typography: Hours and address in body type that remains readable on a phone outdoors.
lessons.media: A place photo is useful when it helps someone recognize the entrance.
lessons.mobile: The address and hours stay above long editorial copy.
lessons.adaptation: If hours conflict in the source, show the conflict rather than picking a convenient value.
lessons.counterexample: A full-screen mood photograph with the address only in the footer.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The visitor who needs to know if the place is open has to hunt.

references.note: Inspected first view: a work photograph with an estimate panel and a phone number in the bar. Demo phone and marketplace banner are not client facts.

lessons.title: Compare options on the decision that matters
lessons.principle: A comparison should use the visitor's actual choice, with differences that change the decision.
lessons.explanation: Three columns of synonyms are not a comparison. Name the criterion, then the difference.
useWhen: The visitor must choose between evidenced options
requiredAssets: Two or more options with factual differences
contraindications: Inventing a competitor or a price
lessons.visitorGoal: Choose an option without guessing which difference matters.
lessons.composition: A table or paired columns keyed to one criterion.
lessons.typography: The criterion labels are as visible as the option names.
lessons.media: Images only when they show the difference.
lessons.mobile: Each option becomes a block that repeats the criterion labels. Do not rely on a wide table alone.
lessons.adaptation: Drop any column that is not backed by a fact.
lessons.counterexample: Three pricing tiers with identical feature lists and a highlighted middle card.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The highlight is a decoration if the features do not differ.

lessons.title: Let a case study change scale on purpose
lessons.principle: A long project page should open with the result, then the constraints, then the work.
lessons.explanation: A case study that repeats the homepage hero wastes the interior's job.
useWhen: A project has enough evidence for a sequence longer than a card
avoidWhen: The only material is a single photo and a title
requiredAssets: A project fact set: situation, work, and outcome
contraindications: No project evidence beyond a title
lessons.visitorGoal: Judge whether a past job resembles their situation.
lessons.composition: Result first, constraints second, process third. Pull quotes only from evidence.
lessons.typography: A readable measure for the narrative. Captions stay with figures.
lessons.media: Place each figure where the paragraph needs it.
lessons.mobile: Figures follow the sentence that introduces them.
lessons.adaptation: If the outcome is unmeasured, do not invent a metric. Describe the visible result.
lessons.counterexample: The homepage hero copied onto the case study with the project name swapped.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The interior then has no job of its own.

lessons.title: Use type to make the first question obvious
lessons.principle: Hierarchy is the difference between the offer, the proof, and the action, not an unusual font.
lessons.explanation: A distinctive typeface can support identity. It does not replace a clear reading order.
useWhen: The identity can be carried by language
Imagery is limited or should stay secondary
avoidWhen: A photographed object is the thing the visitor must recognize immediately
requiredAssets: A specific offer sentence from the narrative
contraindications: Display type set so large that the offer wraps into an unreadable shape
lessons.visitorGoal: Understand the offer in one glance.
lessons.composition: One display line, one supporting sentence, one action. Secondary information steps down.
lessons.typography: Limit the display face to the offer. Body text stays in a readable text face.
lessons.mobile: Shorten the display line rather than shrinking it below the body text.
lessons.adaptation: If the harvested offer is long, split it into a short line and a sentence. Do not invent a slogan.
lessons.counterexample: Three different display faces in one screen, with the action in the same size as the legal text.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: Nothing tells the visitor what to read or do first.

lessons.title: Redraw a complex desktop composition for a narrow screen
lessons.principle: If stacking the desktop regions would scramble the story, specify the mobile order.
lessons.explanation: A side-by-side proof and action can become proof, then action. It should not become action, then an unlabeled image, then the explanation.
useWhen: The desktop composition has two or more regions whose order matters
avoidWhen: The section is already a single column
requiredAssets: A storyboard mobileTransformation for that section
lessons.visitorGoal: Meet the same offer, proof, and action in that order on a phone.
lessons.composition: Name the desktop regions and their mobile sequence.
lessons.typography: Do not let a desktop display size overflow the viewport.
lessons.media: Keep the subject in frame after the crop changes.
lessons.mobile: Write the sequence explicitly: offer, proof, action, or the order this business needs.
lessons.adaptation: Add a 375px check when the transformation is more than a simple stack.
lessons.counterexample: A desktop split that stacks as image, button, then the sentence that explains both.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: The visitor meets the action before they know what it does.

lessons.title: Repeat a treatment only when the items are one list
lessons.principle: Equal cards are appropriate for equal items. They are monotonous when each card has a different job.
lessons.explanation: A menu, a project index, or a comparison can share a template. A homepage that gives the offer, the proof, the process, and the visit the same card does not.
useWhen: Several items share one visitor job
Or a page is starting to repeat unrelated sections
avoidWhen: Using repetition as the only way to fill a homepage
requiredAssets: A storyboard note that says why the repeat exists
contraindications: The repeated sections answer unrelated questions
lessons.visitorGoal: Scan peers quickly, and still see the primary action.
lessons.composition: One template for the list. A different scale for the section that is not part of the list.
lessons.typography: Shared label styles inside the list. A different heading for the section outside it.
lessons.media: Same crop logic inside the list.
lessons.mobile: The list can stack. The primary action does not become just another row.
lessons.adaptation: If the jobs differ, change emphasis or write the rationale that makes them one system.
lessons.counterexample: Five equal card grids for the hero, the story, the hours, the team, and the footer prompt.
lessons.counterexampleWhy: Changing the background color of every other band does not create a new job.
